rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad's sole miracle is the Qur'an, whose clarity and comprehensive ethics suit all peoples and eras and remain unchanged.
rows.anchor: His only miracle was and is the Qur'an itself - a message perfect in its lucidity and ethical comprehensiveness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier prophets served particular communities and eras, so symbolic portents helped people not yet ready for independent thought grasp their mission's truth.
rows.anchor: those prophets stood in need of symbolic portents or miracles

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity had matured enough to grasp an ideology without miracles, which had often produced grave misconceptions in earlier times.
rows.anchor: had reached a degree of maturity which henceforth enabled it to grasp an ideology as such

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The she-camel's origin is not described as miraculous; it was a test for Thamud and a light-giving portent.
rows.anchor: there is absolutely no indication in the Qur'an that the she-camel referred to was of miraculous origin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vision is Muhammad's Ascension, preceded by the Night Journey.
rows.anchor: The vision (ru'ya) mentioned here is the Prophet's experience of the Ascension, preceded by the Night Journey

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its conflicting interpretations test people: shallow believers doubt Muhammad's prophethood, while firm believers see divine grace and grow stronger in faith.
rows.anchor: the weak of faith and the superficial are shaken in their belief in Muhammad's veracity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accursed tree is the zaqqum tree, a manifestation of hell described in 37:62 onward and 44:43 onward.
rows.anchor: spoken of in 37:62 ff. and 44:43 ff. as one of the manifestations of hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is called accursed because it symbolizes hell; hell is singled out here because the passage presents it as a warning.
rows.anchor: it obviously symbolizes hell itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Adam-and-angels allegory is explained at 2:30-34, 7:11-18, and 15:26-41; here its focus is Iblis's contempt for Adam as a metonym for humanity.
rows.anchor: the accent is on the contempt of Iblis for Adam (which is obviously a metonym for the whole human race)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage links Satan's enmity in 17:53 with God's command honoring humanity, developed in 17:70-72.
rows.anchor: this passage apparently connects with the end of verse 53 above

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hanaka literally means putting a rope around a horse's lower jaw; ihtanaka thus means making someone follow submissively or obey blindly.
rows.anchor: he put a rope around the lower jaw (hanak) [of a horse]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about Satan's horses and men is an established metaphor meaning that he uses all his might.
rows.anchor: idiomatically established metaphor, signifying "with all thy might"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's partnership in possessions refers to goods gained or spent sinfully, and in children to conception through fornication or adultery.
rows.anchor: possessions acquired by sinful means or spent on sinful purposes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic ethics and law attach neither moral stigma nor legal disability to a child conceived outside marriage.
rows.anchor: no moral stigma and no legal disability whatever attaches to the child thus begotten

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links this passage to Satan's promise in 4:120.
rows.anchor: Cf. 4:120 and the corresponding note 142.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan has no real power over God's trusting servants, as also stated in 14:22 and 15:42.
rows.anchor: thou shalt have no real power over them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hasib literally describes a stormwind that raises stones, according to Taj al-'Arus.
rows.anchor: Lit., "a stormwind that raises stones" (Taj al-'Arus, art. hasaba).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal wording is therein.
rows.anchor: Lit., "therein".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human dignity rests on conceptual thought, which makes people superior in this respect to other living beings and angels; this continues the theme of verse 61.
rows.anchor: by bestowing upon them the faculty of conceptual thinking

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads imam as the conscious disposition, good or bad, that governs behavior and motivates deeds.
rows.anchor: In his opinion, the expression imdm (lit., "leader" or "guide") has in this context an abstract connotation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad finds Razi's reading most convincing, especially in light of a hadith cited in his note on 53:39.
rows.anchor: This interpretation is most convincing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Receiving the record in the right hand symbolically acknowledges spiritual righteousness; the left hand signifies its opposite.
rows.anchor: A symbolic image, often used in the Qur'an, denoting an acknowledgement of righteousness in the spiritual sense

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that none is wronged applies to righteous and unrighteous alike.
rows.anchor: This last clause obviously applies to both the righteous and the unrighteous.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's rendering of fatil is explained in his note on 4:67.
rows.anchor: For my above rendering of fatil, see surah 4, note 67.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afterlife organically extends earthly life by developing and intensifying tendencies already present here.
rows.anchor: man's life in the hereafter is not merely conditioned by the manner of his life on earth, but is also an organic extension

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh offered to recognize Muhammad as prophet and leader if he acknowledged their tribal gods on God's behalf; he rejected the compromise.
rows.anchor: they demanded of the Prophet that he give some sort of recognition to their tribal deities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's deep faith made it impossible for him to consider the proposed compromise.
rows.anchor: the Prophet's deep faith made it impossible for him to consider anything of this kind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled punishment would be for betraying revelation and misleading followers by example.
rows.anchor: for having gone astray despite the revelation bestowed on thee by God, and for having, by thy example, led thy followers astray as well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beyond the historical event, the passage says a deliberate offense against fundamental truth is unforgivable.
rows.anchor: any conscious offence against a fundamental truth is an unforgivable sin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This Meccan surah was revealed when Quraysh persecution of Muhammad and his followers had reached peak intensity.
rows.anchor: the persecution, both physical and moral, which the Prophet and his followers had to suffer at the hands of the pagan Quraysh reached the peak of its intensity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means after thee.
rows.anchor: Lit., "after thee".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophecy came true just over two years later, when Quraysh leaders were killed at Badr in Ramadan 2 AH.
rows.anchor: This prophecy was fulfilled a little over two years later, in the month of Ramadan, 2 H.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people who expel God's messengers are invariably punished with destruction.
rows.anchor: the people who drove them away were invariably punished with destruction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse, read with the Prophet's practice, establishes the five obligatory daily prayers for adult men and women and their times.
rows.anchor: this verse fully circumscribes the five daily prayers laid down in Islam as obligatory for every adult man and woman

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dawn recitation stands for the morning prayer because the Prophet lengthened its recitation, emphasizing its special significance.
rows.anchor: the Prophet, under divine inspiration, used to lengthen his recitation while praying at that time

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: Most classical commentators understand dawn prayer as witnessed by the angels of both night and day.
rows.anchor: Most of the classical commentators take this to mean

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi identifies the witness as God's illuminating spark in the soul, heightening perception at dawn and enabling spiritual insight through prayer.
rows.anchor: Razi, however, is of the opinion that the "witness" to which the Qur'an refers here is the spark of God-given illumination in man's own soul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night prayer is beyond the five obligatory prayers, so the verse recommends it rather than imposing an obligation.
rows.anchor: in addition to the five obligatory prayers. Hence, the above is not an injunction but a recommendation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet himself regularly spent most of the night in prayer.
rows.anchor: the Prophet himself invariably spent the greater part of the night in prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evildoers are those whose pride or excessive attachment to worldly life makes them reject divine guidance and absolute moral values, ending in spiritual nihilism.
rows.anchor: out of self-conceit or an excessive "love of this world"; reject out of hand any suggestion of divine guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects this description of human response to blessing and hardship with 11:9-10.
rows.anchor: Cf. 11:9-10 and the corresponding notes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means who is best guided on a path.
rows.anchor: as to who is best guided on a path

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators understand ruh here specifically as the revelation of the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: Some commentators are of the opinion that it refers here, specifically, to the revelation of the Qur'an

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Other commentators understand ruh as the human soul.
rows.anchor: others understand by it the "soul", in particular the soul of man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects the soul interpretation because the surrounding verses explicitly concern the Qur'an and divine revelation.
rows.anchor: This latter interpretation is, however, unconvincing inasmuch as the preceding as well as the subsequent verses relate explicitly to the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one could provide the Prophet an alternative guide, since divine revelation is the sole absolute source of ethics.
rows.anchor: divine guidance is the only source of ethics in the absolute sense of this word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking revelation away means removing it from people's hearts and memories as well as erasing it in written form.
rows.anchor: its alienation from the hearts and the memory of men, as well as its disappearance in written form

rows.speaker: Raghib
rows.claim: Raghib treats mathal here as broadly synonymous with wasf, a description by comparison or definition.
rows.anchor: According to Raghib, the noun mathal (lit., "similitude", "parable" or "example") is here more or less synonymous with wasf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In its broadest sense, mathal signifies a lesson.
rows.anchor: In its broadest sense, this term signifies "a lesson".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They refuse ideas that conflict with their own blasphemous inclinations.
rows.anchor: they are unwilling to accept any idea which runs counter to their own, blasphemous inclinations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requested spring is like the one associated with Moses.
rows.anchor: like Moses (cf. 2:60)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demand for a garden and rivers seems to mock the Qur'anic allegory of paradise.
rows.anchor: a derisory allusion to the allegory of paradise so often mentioned in the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word means claimed; the demand may refer to the warning in 34:9.
rows.anchor: possibly a reference to the warning expressed in 34:9

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Suyuti places a response to this demand in 6:7, revealed shortly after the present surah.
rows.anchor: according to Suyuti - shortly after the present surah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demands expose a psychologically contradictory mix of superficial skepticism and primitive credulity, making belief depend on performed miracles.
rows.anchor: a strange mixture of prima-facie scepticism and primitive credulity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Qur'an is Muhammad's only miracle, the demands are irrelevant and frivolous.
rows.anchor: the only miracle granted by God to Muhammad is the Qur'an itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miracles lie solely within God's power, as also stated in 6:109.
rows.anchor: I.e., "miracles are in the power of God alone"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qala and qawl can tropically express holding or asserting a belief; here the statement is a conceptual objection.
rows.anchor: The verb qala (as also the noun qawl) is often used tropically in the sense of holding or asserting an opinion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase for them stresses the individual character of the suffering represented by the blazing flame; see Appendix I for its implications.
rows.anchor: The phrase "for them" is meant, I believe, to stress the individual character of the suffering

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Denying resurrection denies God's power and being; the preceding verse's blindness, deafness, and dumbness characterize this denial.
rows.anchor: this denial of God's power to resurrect the dead (mentioned in exactly the same phrasing in verse 49 of this surah)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creating the dead anew means individually resurrecting each person with the same identity held before death.
rows.anchor: to resurrect them individually, each of them having the same identity (or "likeness") which he or she had before death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ajal means a specified term at which something falls due and here refers to the inevitable resurrection.
rows.anchor: Since ajal denotes, primarily, "a specified term [at which something falls due]", it obviously relates here to the inescapable fact of resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase rendered bounty literally means grace, rahmah.
rows.anchor: Lit., "grace" (rahmah).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans cling instinctively to material goods because they depend on them, while God is self-sufficient and need not limit His bounty; this underscores His guidance through prophets.
rows.anchor: man is, by his very nature, dependent on material possessions, he instinctively tries to hold on to them

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators take the nine clear signs as the miracles performed by Moses.
rows.anchor: Some of the commentators assume that this is an allusion to the miracles performed by Moses

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Other commentators, citing traditions collected by Nasa'i, Ibn Hanbal, Bayhaqi, Ibn Majah, and Tabarani, identify nine specific commands or ethical principles, foremost God's oneness.
rows.anchor: others (relying on a Tradition quoted in the compilations of Nasa'"t, Ibn Hanbal, Bayhagi, Ibn Majah and Tabarani) see in it a reference to nine specific commandments

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad thinks nine may simply be a metonym for several or many, like seven and seventy in classical Arabic.
rows.anchor: the number "nine" may be no more than a metonym for "several"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israelites of the Prophet's time could confirm the Qur'anic account from their scriptures; this explains the later reference in 17:104.
rows.anchor: Ask them about what the Qur'an tells us in this respect, and they will be bound to confirm it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links Moses' appeal here with 7:105, asking Pharaoh to let Israel go.
rows.anchor: let the children of Israel go with me!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad prefers Tabari's reading of mashur as bewitched, given the subsequent mention of Moses' miraculous signs, over his alternative rendering.
rows.anchor: my rendering is based on Tabar-i's interpretation of the passive participle mashar, which I consider preferable

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says lafif describes a crowd made of countless diverse elements, encompassing humankind's varied conditions.
rows.anchor: the expression lafif denotes a human crowd composed of innumerable heterogeneous elements, good and bad, strong and weak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term refutes Israelite hereditary privilege: all humanity will be judged at resurrection, with no people favored in advance.
rows.anchor: on Resurrection Day all mankind will be judged, and none will have a privileged position

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression literally means with truth or in truth.
rows.anchor: Lit., "with truth" or "in truth".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation reached humanity through the Prophet without alteration, omission, or addition.
rows.anchor: it has come down to man, through the Prophet, without any alteration, omission or addition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb can literally mean that the Qur'an was divided into consecutive parts.
rows.anchor: which We have divided into [consecutive] parts

rows.speaker: some authorities quoted by Razi
rows.claim: Some authorities quoted by Razi read the verb as setting the Qur'an forth with clarity.
rows.anchor: according to some authorities (quoted by Razi), "set forth with clarity"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's chosen rendering is meant to preserve both senses.
rows.anchor: The rendering adopted by me allows for both these meanings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's revelation unfolded gradually over the Prophet's 23-year ministry.
rows.anchor: the process of the revelation of the Qur'an was gradual, extending over the twenty-three years of the Prophet's ministry

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although revealed gradually, the Qur'an is one whole and each passage should be read in light of all the others.
rows.anchor: it is nevertheless one integral whole and can, therefore, be properly understood only if it is considered in its entirety

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those endowed with knowledge had received it before the Qur'an came within their awareness.
rows.anchor: before the Qur'an as such has come within their ken

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fulfilled promise may allude to Biblical predictions of Muhammad, especially Deuteronomy 18:15 and 18.
rows.anchor: This may be an allusion to the many Biblical predictions of the advent of the Prophet Muhammad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More broadly, the promise is God's gift of the Qur'an as definitive guidance for humanity's spiritual, cultural, and social development.
rows.anchor: the "fulfilment of God's promise" relates to His bestowal of a definitive revelation, the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-asma al-husna means the most perfect or goodly names.
rows.anchor: the most perfect [or "most goodly"] names

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ar-Rahman is exclusive to God and denotes the unconditional, all-embracing exercise of grace and mercy.
rows.anchor: denoting the unconditional, all-embracing quality and exercise of grace and mercy, and is applied exclusively to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walad primarily means offspring of either sex; present tense expresses God's continuing freedom from the imperfection of begetting.
rows.anchor: the noun walad in its primary sense of "offspring", which applies to a child of either sex

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes the Christian claim that Jesus is God's son and argues that such a relation is logically impossible for God.
rows.anchor: stresses the logical impossibility of connecting such a concept with God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally denies God a protector who could aid Him because of supposed weakness.
rows.anchor: and has no protector [to aid Him] on account of any [supposed] weakness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iwaj can mean crookedness, tortuousness, deviation, distortion, or deviousness.
rows.anchor: The term 'iwaj signifies "crookedness", "tortuousness" or "deviation"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase presents the Qur'an as direct and unambiguous, free of obscurities and internal contradictions, with 4:82 as a parallel.
rows.anchor: meant to establish the direct, unambiguous character of the Qur'an and to stress its freedom from all obscurities and internal contradictions

rows.speaker: most classical commentators and earlier translators
rows.claim: Most classical commentators and earlier translators attach the pronoun to the claim that God took a son, rendering the phrase as lack of knowledge of that event.
rows.anchor: Most of the classical commentators (and, as far as I am aware, all the earlier translators of the Qur'an) relate the pronoun in bihi to the assertion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects that reading because ignorance does not establish that the alleged event objectively did not happen.
rows.anchor: this interpretation is weak inasmuch as absence of knowledge does not necessarily imply an objective negation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads bihi as of Him, referring to God: those making the claim lack real knowledge of Him because they attribute created imperfection to the Supreme Being.
rows.anchor: bihi cannot signify "of it": it signifies "of Him", and relates to God

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari unequivocally supports Asad's reading, while Baydawi gives it as an alternative.
rows.anchor: supported, in an unequivocal manner, by Tabari and, as an alternative, by Baydawi

rows.speaker: Maraghi
rows.claim: Maraghi reads la'alla here as a rhetorical reproach, not an expression of possibility.
rows.anchor: the particle la'alla does not, in this context, indicate a possibility but, rather, a rhetorical question implying a reproach

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question first addresses Muhammad's anguish over Meccan hostility and concern for their spiritual fate.
rows.anchor: the Prophet, who was deeply distressed by the hostility which his message aroused among the pagan Meccans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also applies to anyone convinced of an ethical truth yet dismayed by society's indifference.
rows.anchor: everyone who, having become convinced of the truth of an ethical proposition, is dismayed at the indifference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly adornments test people by revealing their moral character through their attitudes toward material goods and benefits.
rows.anchor: God lets them reveal their real characters in their respective attitudes - moral or immoral - towards the material goods and benefits

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Refusal of spiritual guidance usually stems from blind worldly attachment and pride in one's achievements.
rows.anchor: their excessive, blind attachment to the good of this world, combined with a false pride in what they regard as their own achievements

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's bracketed interpolation supplies the implied link between the preceding verses and the long passage that follows.
rows.anchor: This interpolation establishes the elliptically implied connection between the long passage that follows and the preceding two verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Cave story is not more wondrous than other Qur'anic messages because its parable fits the Qur'an's ethical teaching.
rows.anchor: the allegory or parable based on this story is entirely in tune with the ethical doctrine propounded in the Qur'an as a whole

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators place the story in early Christian history, linking it to Decius's third-century persecution and youths from Ephesus who slept for centuries.
rows.anchor: most of the commentators incline to the view that it relates to a phase in early Christian history - namely, the persecution of the Christians by Emperor Decius in the third century

rows.speaker: most classical commentators
rows.claim: Most classical commentators rely on the Christian legend of the youths and their miraculous sleep to interpret the Qur'anic account.
rows.anchor: the majority of the classical commentators rely on this Christian legend

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad argues that the Christian telling developed from a much older oral tradition with pre-Christian Jewish sources.
rows.anchor: the Christian formulation of this theme is a later development of a much older oral tradition

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir argues that the youths lived before the Christian era, since Jewish rabbis would not preserve a story of Christians after severing friendly relations with them.
rows.anchor: Ibn Kathir remarks in his commentary on verse 13 of this surah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad proposes that the story's fundamentals allegorize the Essene movement, especially the secluded Qumran community; he notes Jesus may have belonged to the Essenes.
rows.anchor: we have before us a striking allegory relating to a movement which played an important role in Jewish religious history

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn 'Abbas and early authorities equate ar-raqim with marqum, something written, and with kitab, scripture.
rows.anchor: some of the earliest authorities - and particularly Ibn 'Abbas - regarded this expression as synonymous with marqum

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi says Arabic rhetoricians and philologists agree that ar-raqim means al-kitab, a writ or scripture.
rows.anchor: Razi adds that "all rhetoricians and Arabic philologists assert that ar-raqim signifies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qumran's scriptural study, copying, preservation, seclusion, and reputation for piety likely inspired the cave-sleep allegory.
rows.anchor: members of the Qumran community - the strictest group among the Essenes - devoted themselves entirely to the study, the copying and the preservation of the sacred scriptures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whatever its origin, the Qur'an uses the story as a parable of resurrection and of faith-driven withdrawal from a wicked world, rewarded by spiritual awakening beyond time and death.
rows.anchor: the fact remains that it is used in the Qur'an in a purely parabolic sense

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording is a rhetorical query introducing a new sentence.
rows.anchor: in the form of a rhetorical query introducing a new sentence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayyin means clear evidence or authority and implies evidence accessible to reason.
rows.anchor: The adjective bayyin ("clear", "obvious", "manifest") implies an evidence accessible to reason

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people either invent imaginary gods, denying God's oneness, or deny God's existence altogether.
rows.anchor: invents imaginary deities and thus gives the lie to the truth of His oneness and uniqueness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story ends abruptly because Qur'anic narratives serve purposes beyond storytelling; here the episode allegorizes death, resurrection, and time as experienced by consciousness.
rows.anchor: revealed in the sequence as an allegory of death and resurrection and of the relativity of "time" as manifested in man's consciousness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future tense in sayaqulun underscores the story's legendary character and makes speculation about details irrelevant to its ethical parable.
rows.anchor: The future tense in sayaqulun points once again to the legendary character of the story as such

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Discussion should be limited to the self-evident ethical lesson of the story, alluding to the first paragraph of 18:21.
rows.anchor: for the sake of the self-evident ethical lesson to be derived from their story
